outputs.label: W

scores.evidence: Opens with a "## Contract" section restating each endpoint, then covers all four sub-concerns: status codes — "POST /v1/orders returns 200 with error in body, not 4xx... **Fix:** Return 400 (bad request) or 422 (unprocessable entity)"; idempotency — "**CRITICAL — Refund endpoint is non-idempotent; retries cause double-charges**... **Fix:** Make refund idempotent using an idempotency key"; pagination — "**HIGH — Unbounded pagination enables expensive queries**... **Fix:** Paginate using cursor (primary key) not offset"; error shape — "Returning `{ "error": "..." }` in a 200 status code means error messages are visible and logged... **Fix:** Return 4xx with generic error message to clients; log detailed error server-side".

Searched for the words "breaking change", "backward", "compat", "migrat", "deprecat", "version", "v2", "sunset", and for any statement that a recommended fix (200 to 4xx, PATCH to merge semantics, ?key= to header) would break partners already integrated, or any discussion of how to roll such a change out. None present. The only uses of "break" are diagnostic descriptions of the current design ('breaks client contracts', 'breaks HTTP semantics'), not a breaking-change or partner-migration concern.

"PATCH /v1/orders/{id} — can caller A modify caller B's order by changing the id? No mention of user ownership checks." and "GET /v1/orders?page=9999999 will scan or fetch 50 orders from a huge offset, or if offset-based, cause full-table scans on the database." and "Nothing prevents a single client from hammering POST /v1/orders or GET /v1/orders?page=1000 continuously."

outputs.notable: Its "Highest-severity issue" section names four issues at once, which defeats the purpose of singling one out. The pagination fix conflates page NUMBER with page SIZE: "Set a max page size (e.g., page 10000 max)" — 10000 is a page index, not a size. Severity taxonomy is inconsistent (CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM, then a stray "WEAK" label). Four items are tagged CRITICAL, which flattens the ranking. The HTTPS item is largely a duplicate of the query-param auth item. Substantively the strongest on adversarial coverage: it is one of only two outputs that catches the IDOR/ownership question across all three mutating or listing endpoints.

outputs.label: X

scores.evidence: Status codes — "**Fix:** Return 400 (Bad Request) or 422 (Unprocessable Entity) with the error body. HTTP 200 means success; errors need appropriate 4xx codes" plus "**Add HTTP status code table** — document all possible responses per endpoint (200, 201, 400, 404, 409, 500, etc.)"; idempotency — "**Fix:** Make refund idempotent — return 200 if already refunded, or reject with 409 (Conflict)... Store refund state on the order"; pagination — "**GET /v1/orders?page=N** lacks: Whether `page` is 1-indexed or 0-indexed... Total count of orders or page count... Whether it's stable (cursor-based pagination is safer for fast-changing data)"; error shape — "**Define error response schema** — how are non-validation errors returned (500s, etc.)?"

Searched for "breaking change", "backward", "compat", "migrat", "sunset", and for any statement about what existing or already-integrated partners would have to change. The nearest text is "**Version the API** — `/v1/` is good; stick with it and document deprecation policy," which recommends having a policy but never names a breaking change, never says which of its own fixes (#1 status codes, #4 PATCH to PUT) is breaking, and never addresses partner integration breakage. Under the no-partial-credit rule this is a gesture, not the item.

Searched for an attacker or a misbehaving partner as an actor: terms "attacker", "abuse", "malicious", "IDOR", "enumerate", "another partner", "caller A / caller B", "ownership", "authorization", "DoS". None appear. The refund defect is framed only as an accident ("can be called twice, causing duplicate refunds"), the auth defect only as passive exposure ("exposes credentials in logs, browser history, and referrer headers"), and rate limiting appears only as a documentation request ("**Add rate limiting info** — how many requests per minute are allowed?"). No concrete misuse path is described.

outputs.notable: Contains a confidently wrong claim: "Query parameters are not private; headers are stripped from logs by standard HTTP tooling." Authorization headers are not reliably stripped anywhere — many gateways, APM agents and debug loggers capture them; the real argument is that URLs are logged by default while headers usually are not. Stating it as a property of "standard HTTP tooling" is an overstatement that could mislead an implementer into thinking a header is inherently safe to log. Also the largest blind spot of the four: no authorization/ownership analysis at all, so it never asks whether a partner can read or refund another partner's orders — arguably the worst defect in a surface about to be handed to third parties. Does deliver a clean go/no-go with named blockers, which the others mostly do too but less crisply.

outputs.label: Y

scores.evidence: Status codes — "200 with `{ "error": "..." }` is not HTTP-compliant. Validation failures must return 4xx (400 Bad Request)"; idempotency — "POST /v1/orders/{id}/refund is not idempotent... Refund operations must be idempotent... (idempotent key pattern, or refund state tracking)"; pagination — "GET /v1/orders?page=N returns 50 items per page, but no metadata about total, has_more, or current_page... **Fix:** Document response structure" with a JSON pagination envelope; error shape — "**5. Insufficient error documentation** ... **Fix:** Document error scenarios" followed by an enumerated code list (`400: validation_error`, `409: order_duplicate`, `500: internal_error`).

"### 10. No versioning deprecation strategy — **Status:** v1 exists, but no plan for v2 or how breaking changes are handled. **Impact:** When you need to change the API, partners won't know what to expect. **Fix:** Publish versioning policy: "Major version bumps for breaking changes (e.g., v2). v1 will be sunset on [DATE] with 12 months notice.""

Searched for "attacker", "abuse", "malicious", "IDOR", "ownership", "authorization", "caller A", "another partner", "enumerate", "scan", "DoS". None appear. Every impact statement is framed as partner inconvenience or accident: the refund defect is "Network retry, browser back-button, or user double-click causes unintended duplicate refunds"; the API-key defect is "API keys will be exposed in logs and caches"; rate limiting is filed under Minor Issues as "Partners don't know how much they can call the API." No concrete misuse-by-an-actor path anywhere.

outputs.notable: Uses "breaking" in two different senses within the same document — "#1, #2, #3, and #4 are breaking problems" in the summary means severe, not backward-incompatible, which muddies the one item it does earn credit for elsewhere. Files "No rate limiting documented" under Minor Issues, framed purely as a partner-expectation gap; for a public partner API the absence of rate limiting is a hardening issue, not documentation polish. Like X, it never raises authorization or per-partner data isolation, so the possibility that any partner key can list or refund any order goes unexamined. The invented error codes (`insufficient_funds`, `order_duplicate`) are presented as examples and read as such, but a careless reader could take them for the real contract. Its "browser back-button" trigger for a duplicate POST refund is a weak mechanism (browsers prompt or re-issue rarely), though retry and double-click are valid.

outputs.label: Z

scores.evidence: Opens with a "## Contract" section that enumerates input, output and side effect per endpoint, marking gaps ("Output: (not specified)"). Status codes — "Should return 400 Bad Request. Status codes are the contract; hiding failure in the body breaks every standard HTTP client and monitoring tool"; idempotency — "**CRITICAL — Refund is non-idempotent.** Calling `POST /v1/orders/{id}/refund` twice refunds twice... **Fix:** make it idempotent... or use an idempotency-key header to deduplicate requests"; pagination — "**MEDIUM — GET pagination unbounded.** No limit on `page=N`... Add `MAX_PAGE=1000` or use cursor-based pagination. Also undocumented: does the sort order change between requests if new orders arrive?"; error shape — "What error shape is returned on non-2xx status codes? (e.g., `{ "error": "...", "code": "..." }` or something else?)" plus "**Fix:** document all response codes and the error shape for each."

Searched for "breaking change", "backward", "compat", "migrat", "deprecat", "version", "v2", "sunset", and for any statement about what already-integrated partners would have to change if these fixes ship. Nothing. The word "breaks" appears once, describing the current design's effect on HTTP clients ("breaks every standard HTTP client and monitoring tool"), not a breaking-change or partner-migration concern. Versioning policy is never mentioned despite the `/v1/` prefix in every path.

"What stops caller A from patching caller B's order? Full-object replacement means overwriting any field (amount, status, owner)." and "**HIGH — No authorization check visible on POST /refund.** Can any authenticated caller refund any order?" and "Caller can request `page=999999` and force a table scan."

outputs.notable: Two terminology errors. It labels unstable pagination ordering "(TOCTOU race)" — that is pagination drift under concurrent inserts, not time-of-check-to-time-of-use. And "move auth to the API boundary (not middleware assumptions)" is confused phrasing; middleware IS a boundary implementation, and the actual point it wants is that the ownership check must exist and be verified rather than assumed. The stray item "✅ **Input validation — assume validated upstream or missing.**" uses a pass marker on something it just said may be absent, which contradicts itself. The page=999999 table-scan claim is asserted without the hedge W applies ("or if offset-based"), so it presumes offset pagination. Strongest of the four on epistemic hygiene: it consistently marks unspecified parts of the contract as unspecified and its "Confirm These" list is framed as assume-no-until-shown, which is the right default for a review of a description rather than code.

methodology_notes:
Item 2 is where my calls could most reasonably have gone the other way, and it drove three of the four scores. The item reads "Flags breaking changes, or explicitly addresses what would break existing partner integrations," but the scenario is a PRE-release partner API, so there are arguably no existing partner integrations to break. That leaves two candidate readings: (a) the output must note that its own recommended fixes (200 to 4xx, PATCH to PUT or merge semantics, moving the key out of the query string) are backward-incompatible and need a rollout, or (b) the output must engage with breaking-change policy for partners at all. I applied (b), the more generous of the two, and still only Y passed, on its item #10 versioning/deprecation section which explicitly names "how breaking changes are handled" and a partner sunset notice. Under reading (a) Y would fail too and all four would be zero on this item, since none of the four says "this fix is breaking, here is how to ship it." I flag that as the single biggest fragility in this scorecard.

The W/X boundary on item 2 is the other close call. X's "Version the API — /v1/ is good; stick with it and document deprecation policy" sits in the same family as Y's #10 but never names a breaking change, never says what partners would have to change, and is one line in a recommendations list. I marked it absent under the explicit no-partial-credit rule. A judge who weighted "document deprecation policy" as sufficient engagement with breaking changes would score X present here, which would put X and Y level on item 2. I do not think that reading survives "a vague gesture in the right direction is absent," but it is defensible.

Item 1 bundles four sub-concerns (status codes, idempotency, pagination, error shape) into one binary. I required all four and all four outputs cleared it, so the item did no discriminating work in this bundle. W was the closest to a miss: its error-shape coverage is framed as an information-leak concern ("error messages are visible and logged... return a generic error message") rather than as an undefined error schema partners must code against, whereas X, Y and Z each explicitly ask for the error schema to be documented. I credited W because it does prescribe what goes in the error body, but a stricter judge reading "error shape as a contract concern" to mean "the response envelope is undefined" could mark W absent. That is the one place I knowingly resolved an ambiguity in an output's favor.

Item 3 was the cleanest to apply. W and Z name actors and mechanisms (caller A patches caller B's order, any authenticated caller refunds any order, page=999999 forces a scan, a single client hammers the endpoint). X and Y describe the same underlying defects but only ever as accidents or passive exposure, with no actor and no misuse path, and neither ever raises authorization or per-partner data isolation. I did not credit "keys will be exposed in logs" as an abuse path, because it names an exposure surface without naming how it is exploited.

One thing the checklist does not capture and which I think matters more than any item on it: X and Y both completely miss the ownership/IDOR question on a surface about to be opened to third parties, while W and Z catch it on all three relevant endpoints. An output can score 2 of 3 here and still be the weaker review.

I did not know and did not try to infer how any output was produced. W/Z and X/Y pair up structurally (contract section plus confirm-list versus numbered severity tiers plus go/no-go), and I scored each of the four against the text independently rather than propagating a score across a pair.
